turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in Mrs Keane, you're very welcome. What has you up to us today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah doctor it's the mornings. I'm wringing with the sweat and shaking like a leaf before the kettle's even on. And the bus, three of them went past full, I was stood there in the rain...
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park the bus. The sweating and the shaking, that's the thing.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The sweating and the shaking, yeah. Nearly every morning. I don't bother with breakfast either, sure I'm not hungry at that hour at all.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mam, stop a second. Doctor, last Tuesday she went confused on me. Didn't know was it Tuesday or Wednesday. Just the once, then she was back.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was grand. I was only half asleep. That neighbour's dog was barking the whole...
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on. Do you remember being muddled yourself?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, not really. Umm. A bit away with the fairies maybe. It passed once I had the tea.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. You're still taking the gliclaside and the metforman, for the diabetes?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I am, yeah. Gliclazide eighty milligrams in the morning. The metformin, I was going to say a gram, but no, it's five hundred twice a day. By mouth, the both of them.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she takes that gliclazide with nothing in her stomach. I've said it to her.

[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so I'm thinking this through. The gliclazide shoves the sugar down whether you've eaten or not. Sweats, a shake, even that one muddle, it would fit a low. I'm not married to it yet.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): A low, is it. My sister Maureen is mad for the biotin, three capsules a day for the hair, says it gives her energy. I told her that's a different thing entirely.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your sister's biotin, we'll leave that with Maureen. Any fever on you these weeks?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Fever? No. Not a temperature.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): And a cough, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. The breathing is grand. The rain though, it was lashing on the...
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the weight, up or down?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I don't know, doctor. Of. The skirts are much the same. Maybe a small bit, maybe nothing. I haven't a scales in the house.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand, we won't put a number on the weight. How long have the morning sweats been going?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh now, the confirmation was lovely, the child's dress had these little pearls...
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mam. He's asking how long.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): About a month, I'd say, the sweats and the shakes. Around then. Not just the day of the party.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): A month. Does the shaking come with the sweat, and does anything ease the two of them?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The shaking comes with the sweat, nearly every morning. Hands going, clammy all over. A cup of tea and a biscuit settles me, if I remember it.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I call in most mornings. She lives on her own since Dad went.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me just see you. Hands are dry sitting here, no shake in them now. Pulse is seventy six. Pressure is one thirty six over eighty two.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not bad, is it. My brother had the diabetes as well, Lord have mercy on him. Always giving out about his own pressure, he was.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note your brother had diabetes. His pressure isn't today's job. For you, I'm calling these morning turns low sugars, provisional mind, until we see the bloods.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods. I hate that yoke in the arm. Do I have to starve for it?

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll do a glucose, an HbA1c, and the kidney bloods. Book the lot at reception on the way out, this week. Come in before breakfast so the glucose means something. The HbA1c doesn't need you fasting.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll have her in Thursday morning, before she eats a thing.

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Leave the doses as they are, eighty of gliclazide in the morning and five hundred of metformin twice a day. But have toast, or anything at all, before that gliclazide. No more skipping the breakfast.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Toast I can manage. I nearly went and bought the biotin like Maureen, but you've said leave it.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave Maureen's biotin, it's nothing to do with your sugars. I'll see you back in a fortnight when the results are in.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, grand. Thanks doctor.

spec.situation: Older diabetic on gliclazide and metformin with morning sweating and shakiness; skips breakfast; daughter reports confusion once; doctor reviews doses and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

omissions.text: Morning sweating/shaking episodes are relieved by a cup of tea and a biscuit; only the shaking entry records the relieving factor, but sweating was also said to settle with tea and a biscuit.
The patient described feeling clammy all over during the morning episodes.
Patient denied any clear weight change / was unsure if weight was up or down ('skirts are much the same', maybe a small bit, maybe nothing).
Confusion episode was also acknowledged by the patient as 'a bit away with the fairies maybe,' not just reported by the caregiver.
Doctor advised to book the blood tests at reception on the way out, this week.
For the planned blood tests, only the glucose was to be done before breakfast/fasting so it 'means something'; HbA1c specifically does not require fasting.

Caregiver reported that the patient takes gliclazide on an empty stomach ('with nothing in her stomach'), which is part of the rationale for suspected low sugars and should be captured as history/corroboration.
Examination finding that the patient's hands were dry while sitting there was not fully captured; only absent hand sweating was recorded.
